## Why Reproducibility Matters

Science is supposed to correct itself: if a finding is real, other researchers should be able to repeat the study and find it again. In the 2010s, researchers tested that promise, and many well-known findings failed. In the largest project, 270 researchers repeated 100 published psychology studies, and fewer than half of them produced the same result a second time ([Open Science Collaboration, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716)). Similar problems were found in medicine, economics, and other fields. This is called the **replication crisis** (or reproducibility crisis).

A *Nature* paper by [Baker (2016)](https://www.nature.com/articles/533452a) states: "More than 70% of researchers have tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiments, and more than half have failed to reproduce their own experiments."

In *Science Fictions*, the psychologist Stuart Ritchie ([2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Fictions)) argues that four problems are behind it: **fraud** (making up data), **bias** (publishing only the results that "worked"), **negligence** (honest mistakes, such as a typo in a spreadsheet or a number copied incorrectly into a paper), and **hype** (claiming more than the results show). Most researchers will never commit fraud. Negligence is different: anyone can copy the wrong number into a table, forget which version of the data they used, or lose track of how a variable was cleaned.

A reproducible report is your protection against negligence. In a Quarto report, the plots, tables, and numbers are made by code, in the same file as your writing. Nothing is copied and pasted by hand. Anyone who has your data file and your `.qmd` file can run the report and get the same results, including you, six months from now.

A primary objective of this playbook is to increase the reproducibility of public health research using line-by-line coding in R with Quarto for publishing the research with code chunks to confirm accuracy.

## Reproducible Reports

Students on the quantitative and mixed-methods data analysis tracks will produce a reproducible Quarto Markdown report  for your individual report. You will learn how to start your own Quarto report later, in [Start a Report](codechunks.qmd). Right now, you do not need any software. Peruse a range of individual and team manuscripts that were published as Quarto reports.

### Quarto Examples

Quarto provided two examples of a reproducible report and manuscript:

-   [Standard Quarto Report Example](https://quarto-dev.github.io/quarto-gallery/page-layout/tufte.html)

-   [Standard Quarto Manuscript Example](https://quarto-ext.github.io/manuscript-template-jupyter/)

### FRI-PH Cohort 11 Examples

FRI-PH Cohort 11 produced individual reports and a team manuscript. Cohort 12 will ONLY produce an individual report. Below are examples of individual reports from students: 

-   [Individual Report on Sleep](https://danicalyktey.quarto.pub/sleep/)

-   [Individual Report on Cooking Self-Efficacy](https://yoominkim.quarto.pub/indvidualfinalreport/)

-   [Team Manuscript on Violence Prevention](https://vraposo.quarto.pub/mixed-methods-analysis-of-preferences-for-community-based-violence-prevention-and-intervention-approaches/)

- [Team Manuscript on Veggies](https://avishnevetsk.quarto.pub/is-the-binghamton-community-eating-enough-vegetables/)

### FRI-PH Lab Examples

The FRI Public Health Lab has produced Quarto manuscripts from active research projects:

-   [Health Avoiders Manuscript](https://zihanhei.quarto.pub/avoider-report/)

-   [Zero Sum Full Manuscript](https://fripublichealth.quarto.pub/zerosum/)

-   [Zero Sum Mini Manuscript](https://fripublichealth.quarto.pub/zerosum/example-preview.html)
